headline_findings: This comparison covers two papers - one on Lyme disease and one on Long COVID - and does not describe either condition in general.

The Lyme disease paper quantifies diagnostic delay, travel burden, hospital access difficulty, and insurance/disability denial, while the Long COVID paper quantifies excess incidence and risk factors but reports no comparable access-barrier or administrative-denial figures.
Neither paper reports direct dollar cost, out-of-pocket cost, or productivity-loss figures, so no cost-based comparison can be made between the two conditions studied here.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that 37.5 percent of surveyed patients saw 10 or more physicians before being diagnosed, reflecting substantial diagnostic delay in its self-selected chronic-Lyme sample.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not report a diagnostic-delay figure; it only notes as an unquantified limitation that patients must seek care for a diagnosis to be documented in electronic health records.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Diagnostic delay is directly measured in one paper and not in the other, so readers should not assume the two conditions are comparable on this point.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper finds 49.5 percent of patients traveled more than 50 miles for treatment and 81.7 percent of those who sought local hospital care reported difficulty obtaining it.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not quantify any access-barrier figure; it only mentions healthcare access variation by gender, race/ethnicity, and rurality as an unquantified limitation.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Lyme disease paper provides numeric access-barrier figures, so no side-by-side access comparison is possible here.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports an insurance-denial-minus-disability-denial gap of 1.3 percentage points, with 39.9 percent of insurance applicants denied new coverage and 38.6 percent of disability applicants denied benefits tied to non-conformity with IDSA treatment guidelines.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not tag an administrative-barrier category and reports no insurance-denial or disability-denial figures.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Administrative denial is a documented burden only in the Lyme disease paper, which matters for anyone comparing coverage-related obstacles across the two conditions.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper collected no dollar cost figures itself; it cites an outside 2006 study only for context and explicitly says that study should not be pooled with its own survey percentages.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports no direct medical cost, out-of-pocket cost, or productivity-loss figures of any kind, stating this would require an entirely separate cost dataset.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers leave direct cost evidence completely unmeasured, so neither can support a dollar-based burden claim for its condition.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper mentions job loss only by citing a separate, smaller 1993 survey for context; its own 2009-2010 survey did not measure job loss or income loss.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not mention work loss, income loss, or productivity loss anywhere in its findings.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Even the Lyme disease paper's job-loss mention is secondhand rather than self-measured, and the Long COVID paper has nothing at all on this dimension, so work/income loss is essentially absent from both papers' own data.

comparison_rows.dimension: How official data may undercount each condition

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper cites, as background context, the CDC's acknowledged 6- to 12-fold underreporting multiplier applied to 2008 case counts (35,198 reported versus an estimated 200,000-400,000 cases), but this figure comes from the CDC, not from the survey's own data collection.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper's own analysis is tagged surveillance_undercount: it computes excess incidence attributable to COVID-19 of 5.3 percentage points in the N3C network's data and 6.3 percentage points in the PCORnet network's data, while its claims_undercounting limitation notes that electronic-health-record-based detection may produce lower or different counts in the setting studied.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: The two papers handle official undercounting differently: the Lyme disease paper cites an external CDC adjustment factor as context, while the Long COVID paper computes its own excess-incidence estimates directly within its analysis, so the figures are not on the same footing.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper's own evidence gaps state it collected no caregiver-time, family-burden, or lifetime-cost-trajectory data, and no breakdown by age, gender, socioeconomic status, or ethnicity.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper's own evidence gaps state it has no patient-reported outcome or chart-review validation, no follow-up beyond 180 to 270 days, and no cost data of any kind.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers leave substantial aspects of burden unmeasured, which limits how far either can be generalized beyond its own sample and method.

shared_themes.theme: Neither paper provides direct dollar cost figures for the condition it studies, relying instead on percentages, counts, or external citations for cost context.

evidence.note: This paper's survey collected only access and utilization percentages, with Zhang et al. 2006 dollar figures cited externally, not computed by the survey itself.
This paper reports incidence and risk-factor figures only, explicitly stating no cost, productivity-loss, or caregiving-burden data are included.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers describe a systemic gap tied to inconsistent or contested standards for defining or classifying the condition, which the papers' authors say affects how patients are identified or treated.

evidence.note: This paper describes IDSA treatment guidelines functioning as de facto policy across hospital credentialing, insurance coverage, and disability determinations, independent of individual clinical presentation.

This paper describes the lack of a gold-standard case definition for Long COVID, with three EHR networks each using a different computable phenotype and published estimates ranging from 6 percent to over 50 percent.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper quantifies patient-reported diagnostic delay, travel burden, hospital access difficulty, and insurance/disability denial tied to guideline non-conformity.

evidence.note: Reports 37.5 percent seeing 10+ physicians before diagnosis, 49.5 percent traveling over 50 miles for treatment, 81.7 percent reporting hospital-access difficulty, and 38.6 percent of disability applicants denied for non-conformity with IDSA guidelines.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Long COVID paper identifies demographic and clinical risk factors (sex, age, acute illness severity) for developing the condition, a type of finding the Lyme disease paper does not provide.

evidence.note: Reports adjusted hazard ratios including 1.78 for age 65+ (N3C) and 2.83 for ICU-level hospitalization in children (PEDSnet), identifying who faces higher risk of developing Long COVID.

evidence_gaps_shared: Neither paper provides direct medical cost, out-of-pocket cost, or productivity-loss figures, so no dollar-based burden comparison is possible between the two conditions studied here.
Neither paper's findings are broken down by age, gender, socioeconomic status, race/ethnicity, or rurality into disaggregated figures, though both note this as a limitation of their own data.
cross_analysis.summary: This comparison covers two papers, one built from a 2009-2010 patient survey on chronic Lyme disease and one built from a 2025 electronic-health-record incidence study on Long COVID. The Lyme disease paper quantifies diagnostic delay, travel burden, hospital-access difficulty, and insurance or disability denial directly from patient-reported survey data, while the Long COVID paper quantifies excess incidence and clinical/demographic risk factors directly from EHR-based computable phenotypes. Neither paper reports direct dollar costs, out-of-pocket costs, or productivity-loss figures, and both flag unresolved issues with case definitions or guideline enforcement as a systemic limitation on their own findings. Because each paper uses a different data source, population, and measurement approach, the figures shown here describe what each paper separately reports and should not be read as a controlled comparison of the two conditions.
cross_analysis.limitations: This analysis rests on a small, non-random set of papers: exactly one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper, each built from a single uploaded document with its own self-selected or network-specific sample, so no conclusions about either condition in general can be drawn, and findings on dimensions not covered by either paper's own data cannot be filled in or inferred.

learning_cards.headline: Long COVID could track how many clinicians patients see before diagnosis.
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper reports 37.5 percent of patients saw 10+ physicians before diagnosis.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper measures excess incidence from EHR data but does not report how many clinicians patients saw before diagnosis.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers add a measure of the number of clinicians seen before diagnosis to their EHR-based studies?

learning_cards.headline: Travel distance and hospital access trouble are measurable, worth tracking.
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper found 49.5 percent of patients traveled over 50 miles for treatment and 81.7 percent reported difficulty obtaining hospital treatment.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper's EHR-based incidence figures do not capture travel distance or self-reported difficulty accessing hospital care.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers survey patients about travel distance and hospital-access difficulty alongside their incidence estimates?

learning_cards.headline: Insurance versus disability denial gaps are worth measuring too.
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper found insurance denial was 1.3 percentage points more common than disability-benefit denial.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper's incidence-based figures do not include any measure of insurance or disability-benefit denial rates.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers compare insurance denial rates to disability-benefit denial rates for their patients?

learning_cards.headline: EHR-based excess-incidence estimates could reveal hidden Lyme undercount.
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper reports excess incidence attributable to COVID-19 of 5.3 percentage points (N3C adults), 6.3 percentage points (PCORnet adults), and 1.4 percentage points (PEDSnet children).
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper's 2009-2010 survey data does not include any EHR-based population-level incidence or undercount estimate.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Lyme disease researchers apply similar EHR-based excess-incidence methods to estimate how much chronic Lyme disease is undercounted?

learning.takeaway: The Lyme disease paper shows how patient-reported access and administrative barriers can be measured directly, while the Long COVID paper shows how EHR-based incidence methods can estimate undercounted burden; each could borrow the other's measurement approach to help fill its own gaps.
